Isocitric acid can form salts and esters known as isocitrates. Its anion form is an intermediate in the citric acid cycle.

scheda_en.intro:
Isocitric acid is a structural isomer of citric acid and consequently shares similar physical and chemical properties. This makes it difficult to separate the two isomers. Isocitric acid can form salts and esters known as isocitrates. Its anion form is an intermediate in the citric acid cycle.
Isocitric acid is commonly used as a marker to detect the authenticity and quality of fruit products, most often citrus juices.  In authentic orange juice, for example, the ratio of citric acid to D-isocitric acid is usually less than 130. An isocitric acid value higher than this may be indicative of fruit juice adulteration.
Isocitric acid has largely been used as a biochemical agent due to limited amounts. However, isocitric acid has been shown to have pharmaceutical and therapeutic effects. Isocitric acid has been shown to effectively treat iron deficient anemia. Additionally, isocitric acid could be used to treat Parkinson's disease. Yarrowia lipolytica can be used to produce isocitric acid and is inexpensive compared to other methods. Furthermore, other methods produce unequal amounts of citric acid to isocitric acid ratio, mostly producing citric acid. Use of Yarrowia lipolytica produces a better yield, making equal amounts of citric acid to isocitric acid.
scheda_en.chimica: **Citric Acid Cycle.** Isocitrate is the intermediate in the citric acid cycle between citrate and α-ketoglutarate. Citrate covalently interacts with the iron-sulfur core of aconitase. The enzyme's core also controls the reversible addition or removal of H2O from the molecule. In the transition between citrate and isocitrate, H2O is temporarily added to the substrate to create the intermediate molecule, cis-aconitate. The intermediate can exist as aconitic acid, but in the citric acid cycle, it does not dissociate from the enzyme and proceeds directly to the next structure when H2O is removed from the molecule. Although the ΔG′°=13.3 kJ/mol, an unfavorable value, the isocitrate concentration is constantly lowered by its transformation into α-ketoglutarate. The transformation between isocitrate and α-ketoglutarate has an intermediate, the enol, oxalosuccinate and is catalyzed by isocitrate dehydrogenase. The enzyme contains an Mn2+ which stabilizes and interacts with the intermediate. After isocitrate is oxidized into oxalosuccinate, it is decarboxylated and rearranged into α-ketoglutarate and continues in the citric acid cycle.
